tables.how: From each of the Foundation's 5 returns on file (tax years ending 2021 to 2025): the line on which it reports its dealings with a related organization, and its total expenses. Beside them, the matching line on the Alliance's own return for the same year and, for the two years it covers, the figure in the Alliance's audited statements. The case's 81% and 91% are the first line divided by total expenses: 81.2% for the year to June 2024 and 91.5% for the year to June 2025. The two organizations' returns give the same amount in every year. In 1 year (2023) the amount paid is larger than the Foundation's total expenses, so the two lines are not measured the same way. The returns give the filer's name as “UNION SQUARE BUSINESS IMPROVEMENT DISTRICT” and “UNION SQUARE BUSINESS IMPROVEMENT DISTRICT dba UNION SQUARE ALLIANCE”; they are one organization's by their employer identification number, 94-3159152.
tables.limits: A charity that has no staff of its own and pays a related district to run its programs is an ordinary arrangement: a charity can receive grants and gifts that a business district cannot. The line gives one amount for the year and does not split a management fee from program money, and it does not show that City grant money, rather than donations, is what was paid on. Money the Foundation pays on to the Alliance is not money it spends on itself. A tax return is the organization's own statement, signed under penalty of perjury and not audited by the IRS. Its tax year is often not the City's fiscal year, and it counts money when earned or spent under its accounting method, not when the City paid. A disclosure on a return, including a dealing with an officer or a director, is what the law requires to be reported; the question is whether it is fair and approved.

tables.how: Fiscal 2019 to fiscal 2026, to the cent. The Alliance is paid under the City's spelling “Union Square Business Improvmnt District”. Payments to it from “General City - Unallocated” are the district's own property assessments, which the City collects and hands over: $50,003,599.71 of the $52,876,743.39 it received. The rest, $2,873,143.68, is City grants and contracts. The Foundation received $5,467,162.49, all of it grants. In fiscal 2025 the Foundation was paid $1,506,172.49 and the Alliance $7,658,746.67, of which $7,123,362.67 was assessments. The City's list of benefit districts gives the district's yearly assessment revenue as $6,858,146; the audit gives $7,081,504 for the year to June 2025. Each organization's payments in the two tables the Controller publishes, as retrieved on 12 November 2026: Citywide Nonprofit Spending, which by its own description keeps contracted services only, and Vendor Payments (Vouchers), the table of every payment. The fiscal year is the one printed on the payment. Payee names are matched by the rule the organization pages use: the name without punctuation and company suffixes, plus the renames and spellings that a shared contract number confirms.
tables.limits: An assessment handed over is the property owners' own money, not a City grant, and the nonprofit-spending table rightly leaves it out. Two City payment streams to two related organizations do not show that any work was paid for twice: that would need the invoices under each grant, which are not public data. A payment is money the City sent, not money the organization kept or spent on itself: subsidies, rent aid and grants that an organization pays on to others are in these figures. The two tables differ where the nonprofit-spending table leaves out a kind of payment or a contract; neither is wrong for that reason. The year printed on a payment can be later than the year the payment was issued. A payee the City spells in a way that no contract number ties to the organization is not counted.
